title: Linux Mastery
subtitle: Zero to DevOps-ready: 19 modules, every topic, hands-on labs, interview proof

phases.name: Foundations
phases.tagline: What Linux is and how to talk to it

modules.name: Linux Foundations
modules.summary: What an OS, kernel, shell, and distribution actually are.

subtopics.name: OS as hardware manager
points: Sits between hardware and applications, abstracting CPU, memory, and devices
Without an OS every program would need its own hardware drivers
Provides four core services: process scheduling, memory management, filesystem, device I/O

subtopics.name: OS as resource allocator
points: Decides which program runs on the CPU and when (scheduling)
Isolates processes so one crashing program cannot take down others
Enforces access control on files, devices, and network resources

subtopics.name: OS examples
points: Linux, Windows, macOS are general-purpose operating systems
Android is built on the Linux kernel; iOS on the Darwin/XNU kernel
Servers overwhelmingly run Linux for stability, cost, and automation

subtopics.name: What the kernel does
points: Privileged core program with direct hardware access
Manages processes, memory pages, filesystems, and device drivers
Exposes hardware to programs through system calls (open, read, write, fork)

subtopics.name: Kernel space vs user space
points: Kernel space: privileged mode, direct hardware access, a crash here panics the system
User space: restricted mode where applications and shells run
System calls are the controlled bridge between the two worlds

subtopics.name: Monolithic design
points: Linux is monolithic: core services share one kernel address space for speed
Drivers load and unload at runtime as kernel modules (lsmod)
Contrast with microkernels where services run as separate user-space servers

subtopics.name: Shell
points: Command interpreter that reads input and launches programs (Bash, zsh, fish)
Expands wildcards, variables, quoting, pipelines, and redirection before execution
Also a scripting language — the same syntax automates servers

subtopics.name: Terminal
points: Application window rendering text and forwarding keystrokes (GNOME Terminal, xterm)
Historically a physical device; today a terminal emulator program
The shell runs INSIDE the terminal — they are two different layers

subtopics.name: Console
points: The physical or primary virtual I/O directly attached to a machine
On servers often reached via serial console or IPMI when nothing else works
Kernel panic messages appear on the console — the last resort display

subtopics.name: CLI strengths
points: Scriptable: the same command runs on 1 server or 1000 identically
Low bandwidth and precise — works over slow SSH links
Every action is reproducible, loggable, and version-controllable

subtopics.name: GUI strengths
points: Discoverable: menus reveal what is possible without memorization
Better for one-off visual tasks like image editing
Costs RAM, CPU, and attack surface — a liability on servers

subtopics.name: Server reality
points: Most Linux servers run headless with no GUI installed
DevOps work is CLI-first: SSH sessions, config files, automation
Learn the CLI deeply; treat GUI tools as optional conveniences

subtopics.name: What a distro is
points: Linux kernel + GNU tools + package manager + installer + defaults, bundled by a vendor or community
Same kernel family, different tooling, release cadence, and support model
Choosing a distro mostly means choosing a package manager and lifecycle

subtopics.name: Major families
points: Debian family (Debian, Ubuntu, Mint): apt/dpkg, .deb packages
RHEL family (RHEL, Fedora, Rocky, AlmaLinux): dnf/yum/rpm, .rpm packages
Arch family (Arch, Manjaro): pacman, rolling release
Others: openSUSE (zypper), Alpine (apk — tiny, container favorite)

subtopics.name: Which to learn
points: Ubuntu/Debian: beginner-friendly, huge community, dominant in cloud
RHEL/Rocky/Alma: enterprise standard and the RHCSA certification target
Learn one deeply, then map concepts — 90% of Linux knowledge transfers

subtopics.name: The naming truth
points: Linux strictly means the kernel, started by Linus Torvalds in 1991
GNU (Richard Stallman, 1983) wrote the userland: gcc, bash, coreutils
A distro is GNU tools + Linux kernel — hence the name GNU/Linux

subtopics.name: Unix roots
points: Linux is Unix-like: follows POSIX conventions but contains no AT&T Unix code
Inherits the Unix philosophy: small composable tools, text streams, everything is a file
POSIX compliance is why skills transfer across Linux, macOS, and BSD

subtopics.name: Open-source licensing
points: Linux is GPLv2: free to use, modify, and distribute, with source included
Copyleft: derivative works must also ship their source code
This license is why thousands of companies contribute to a single kernel

modules.lab: Run uname -r, cat /etc/os-release, and hostnamectl on your machine. Then run man uname and identify which flag prints only the kernel release versus all information.
modules.lab_expected: You can state your distro name/version, kernel version, and hostname; man <command> becomes your first reflex when unsure.
modules.interview_q: What is the difference between Linux and Unix? What is the Linux kernel?
modules.interview_a: Linux is a Unix-like open-source kernel; Unix is a family of proprietary operating systems sharing design conventions. The kernel is the privileged core program managing hardware, processes, memory, and filesystems — everything else (shell, tools, desktop) runs in user space.

modules.name: The Shell
modules.summary: Command anatomy, paths, completion, history, and getting help.

subtopics.name: Role of the shell
points: Reads each line you type, parses it, and launches the requested program
Handles wildcards, variables, quoting, redirection, and pipelines before the program runs
Returns the program's exit code so scripts can branch on success or failure

subtopics.name: Common shells
points: Bash: default on most distros, POSIX-compatible with extensions
zsh: popular interactive shell with richer completion and themes
sh/dash: minimal POSIX shell, often what /bin/sh points to for fast scripts
fish: friendly interactive shell but not POSIX-compatible — scripts may break

subtopics.name: command [options] [arguments]
points: Example: ls -l /etc — command=ls, option=-l, argument=/etc
Options modify behavior; arguments are the targets acted upon
Order matters for some tools — options usually come before arguments

subtopics.name: Short vs long options
points: Single dash bundles single letters: ls -lah
Double dash uses readable words: ls --all --human-readable
Use -- to mark end of options: rm -- -weirdfile handles dash-prefixed names

subtopics.name: Absolute paths
points: Start at root: /etc/nginx/nginx.conf — works from any directory
Unambiguous and stable — preferred in scripts, cron jobs, and configs
Longer to type but never depend on where you currently are

subtopics.name: Relative paths
points: Resolved from the current directory: ../logs/app.log
. means current directory, .. means the parent directory
Shorter interactively but break if you cd elsewhere — a classic script bug

subtopics.name: Tab completion
points: Tab auto-completes commands, paths, and even option names
Double-Tab lists all matches when the input is ambiguous
Fastest way to avoid typos in long paths — build the muscle memory

subtopics.name: Command history
points: Up arrow or the history command recalls previous commands
Ctrl+R reverse-searches history incrementally as you type
!n re-runs command number n; !! repeats the last command; !$ reuses its last argument

subtopics.name: man pages
points: man <command> is the authoritative reference, organized in numbered sections
Navigate with / to search and q to quit
man 5 passwd (file format) vs man 1 passwd (command) — section numbers disambiguate

subtopics.name: Quick help tools
points: <command> --help prints a concise option summary — try this first
whatis gives a one-line description; apropos searches descriptions by keyword
type tells whether a name is a builtin, alias, function, or external binary

modules.lab: From your home directory, cd to /etc using an absolute path, list only hidden files there, then return home with a bare cd. Use history to find your ls command number and re-run it with !<number>.
modules.lab_expected: You move between directories without thinking, and use tab-completion and history instead of retyping.
modules.interview_q: What shell are you using and how do you check? What is the difference between which, type, and whereis?
modules.interview_a: echo $0 or echo $SHELL shows the current shell. which searches PATH for external binaries only; type also reports shell builtins, keywords, functions, and aliases; whereis additionally lists man pages and source locations.

phases.name: File Mastery
phases.tagline: Files, permissions, users, processes, text — the daily toolkit

modules.name: Filesystem Hierarchy & File Operations
modules.summary: The filesystem tree, file types, inodes, links, and file operations.

subtopics.name: One root to rule them all
points: Everything hangs under one root / — no drive letters like Windows C:
Other disks and partitions are grafted onto the tree via mounting at any directory
This uniformity is why the same tools work on local disks, USB sticks, and network shares

subtopics.name: Path resolution
points: Absolute paths always start with / and work from anywhere
Relative paths resolve from the current working directory (see pwd)
The kernel resolves each path component left to right through directory entries

subtopics.name: System binaries
points: /bin: essential user commands (ls, cp, mv) needed even in single-user mode
/sbin: system administration binaries (fdisk, iptables, reboot)
Modern distros often merge these into /usr/bin via symlinks — know both layouts

subtopics.name: Configuration and variable data
points: /etc: host-specific configuration files — the admin's main workplace
/var: data that grows — logs (/var/log), mail spools, caches, databases
Rule: /etc is edited by humans, /var is written by programs

subtopics.name: Homes and temporary space
points: /home: user home directories — each user's private space
/root: root's home, kept separate so /home can fail or be unmounted independently
/tmp: world-writable scratch space, often cleared on reboot (tmpfs)
/opt: third-party commercial software bundles living outside the package manager

subtopics.name: System and virtual directories
points: /usr: shareable read-only programs, libraries, and documentation
/boot: kernel images, initramfs, and bootloader configuration
/lib: shared libraries needed at boot; /lib64 on 64-bit systems
/dev: device files; /proc: live kernel and process info; /sys: kernel object model — virtual, zero disk usage

subtopics.name: The philosophy
points: Devices, processes, sockets, and kernel tunables all appear as files
One toolset (cat, echo, grep) manages wildly different resources uniformly
Writing to the right file can reconfigure hardware — with great power comes rm -rf

subtopics.name: Concrete examples
points: /dev/sda is a disk you can read block by block
/proc/cpuinfo exposes CPU details as readable text
/sys/class/net/eth0/ holds live network interface state and tunables

subtopics.name: Type characters in ls -l
points: - regular file, d directory, l symbolic link
b block device (disks), c character device (terminals, /dev/null)
p named pipe (FIFO), s Unix domain socket

subtopics.name: Inodes
points: Metadata structure holding size, owner, permissions, timestamps, and block pointers
Stores everything about a file EXCEPT its name — names live in directory entries
Finite supply: df -i shows usage; exhaust inodes and no new files can be created despite free space

subtopics.name: Hard links
points: Another directory entry pointing to the same inode — same file, two names
Restricted to one filesystem; cannot link directories (normally)
Deleting one name leaves the data intact until the last link is removed
Created with ln (no -s); verify with ls -li showing identical inode numbers

subtopics.name: Soft (symbolic) links
points: A separate small file storing a path to the target — shown as name -> target
Can cross filesystems and point to directories
Breaks (dangles) if the target moves or is deleted
Created with ln -s; most config management uses symlinks for version switching

subtopics.name: Create and navigate
points: mkdir -p builds nested directory trees in one shot
touch creates empty files or updates timestamps on existing ones
cd, pwd, and ls are the movement trio — learn their flags cold

subtopics.name: Copy, move, delete
points: cp -r copies trees; -a (archive) preserves permissions, timestamps, and links
mv renames or relocates — atomic within one filesystem
rm -r deletes trees, -i prompts, -f forces; rm -rf with a wrong path destroys data — always echo the path first

subtopics.name: Inspect and find
points: file identifies content type regardless of extension
stat shows full inode metadata: blocks, links, access/change/modify times
find . -name '*.log' -type f -mtime -7 locates files by name, type, and age

modules.lab: Build ~/lab3/projects/{alpha,beta}/docs with one command. Create notes.txt in docs, copy it to alpha, move the copy to beta, create a symlink to it in your home dir, then delete the whole lab3 tree. Inspect with ls -li to compare inode numbers of the hard vs soft link.
modules.lab_expected: You create nested trees fast, and can explain from inode numbers why a hard link shares an inode while a symlink does not.
modules.interview_q: What is the difference between a hard link and a soft (symbolic) link? What is an inode?
modules.interview_a: A hard link is another directory entry pointing to the same inode — same filesystem only, survives original deletion. A symlink is a separate file holding a path — can cross filesystems but breaks if the target moves. An inode stores all file metadata (size, permissions, timestamps, block locations) except the name.

modules.name: Permissions
modules.summary: Reading and setting permissions: rwx, chmod, umask, and special bits.

subtopics.name: Field by field
points: Format: type+perms, link count, owner, group, size, timestamp, name
Example: -rwxr-xr-- 1 ashu dev 2048 Oct 10 notes.txt — decode each field on sight
First character is the type: - file, d directory, l symlink

subtopics.name: Link count, owner, and timestamps
points: Second field is the hard-link count — directories always show at least 2 (. and itself)
Owner and group columns show who controls the file — change with chown/chgrp
Timestamp shows mtime by default; ls -lu shows access time, --time-style=full-iso gives precision

topics.name: rwx meaning for files vs directories

subtopics.name: On files
points: r: read the file's contents
w: modify or truncate the file's contents
x: execute the file as a program or script

subtopics.name: On directories
points: r: list the names inside the directory
w: create, delete, and rename entries inside it
x: enter the directory and access its contents — the real gatekeeper
Classic trap: r without x shows names but opens nothing

subtopics.name: Symbolic mode
points: chmod u+x file adds execute for the owner; go-w removes write for group+others
chmod a=r file sets everyone to read-only in one stroke
Readable and surgical — best for small permission tweaks

subtopics.name: Numeric (octal) mode
points: r=4, w=2, x=1; sum per class: 7=rwx, 6=rw-, 5=r-x, 4=r--, 0=---
chmod 755 = rwxr-xr-x; memorize the common set below
Everyday values: 644 files, 755 directories and scripts, 600 secrets, 700 private dirs

subtopics.name: Ownership with chown/chgrp
points: chown user:group file changes owner and group — requires root
chgrp group file changes only the group
Everyday pattern: chown -R app:app /srv/app after deploying

subtopics.name: The concept
points: umask is a subtractive filter masking bits OFF new files and directories
Base permissions: files start at 666, directories at 777, then umask removes bits
It never ADDS permissions — only takes away

subtopics.name: The math
points: umask 022 → files 644, directories 755 (the common default)
umask 027 → files 640, directories 750 (group-private default)
umask 077 → files 600, directories 700 (paranoid default)
Check with umask; set persistently in ~/.bashrc

subtopics.name: setuid (4xxx)
points: Program runs with the FILE OWNER's privileges, not the runner's
Example: /usr/bin/passwd runs as root so users can change their own password
Shown as s in the owner-x position: -rwsr-xr-x; audit with find / -perm -4000

subtopics.name: setgid (2xxx)
points: On files: runs with the file GROUP's privileges
On directories: new files inherit the directory's group — the shared-project pattern (chmod 2770)
Shown as s in the group-x position

subtopics.name: Sticky bit (1xxx)
points: On world-writable directories: only the file's owner (or root) may delete or rename
/tmp is the classic: drwxrwxrwt (1777) — everyone writes, nobody deletes others' files
Shown as t in the other-x position

subtopics.name: Why 777 is dangerous
points: Gives everyone read, write, AND execute — any user can modify or replace the content
On scripts or web roots it enables code injection by any local account
Fix is almost always 755 (dirs) or 644 (files), tightened per actual need

modules.lab: Create ~/lab4/secret.txt and ~/lab4/shared/. Set secret.txt to 600, shared/ to 770, then set the setgid bit on shared/ (chmod 2770). Change your umask to 027, create a new file, and verify it was created as 640. Finally, explain why /tmp has permissions 1777.
modules.lab_expected: You fluently convert between rwxr-xr-- and 754; you can predict default file/dir permissions from a umask; you know setuid (4xxx), setgid (2xxx), sticky (1xxx) and their use cases.
modules.interview_q: Explain chmod 4755, the sticky bit on /tmp, and what umask 022 does.
modules.interview_a: 4755 = setuid + rwxr-xr-x: the program executes with the file owner's privileges. The sticky bit on world-writable /tmp means only each file's owner (or root) can delete it. umask 022 strips write for group and others, so new files are 644 and new directories 755.

modules.name: Users & Groups
modules.summary: Creating and managing users and groups, and where accounts live.

subtopics.name: Identity model
points: Every process runs as a numeric UID; every file is owned by a UID and GID
Usernames and group names are friendly labels over the numbers (see id)
UID 0 is root: bypasses all permission checks — use sparingly and never for daily work

subtopics.name: Groups
points: Collections of users used to grant shared access to files
Each user has exactly one primary group and any number of secondary groups
New files take the user's primary group unless a directory setgid bit overrides it

subtopics.name: /etc/passwd
points: One line per user: name:x:UID:GID:comment:home:shell
World-readable by design; the x means the password hash lives in /etc/shadow
The shell field controls login ability — /usr/sbin/nologin disables interactive login

subtopics.name: /etc/shadow
points: Hashed passwords plus aging fields (last change, min/max age, warn, expire)
Readable only by root — this split is why shadow exists
!! or * in the hash field means the account cannot authenticate with a password

subtopics.name: /etc/group
points: Group definitions: name, GID, and member list
Secondary memberships are recorded here, not in passwd
Read it directly to audit who belongs where

subtopics.name: Creating
points: useradd -m -s /bin/bash deployer creates the user with a home dir and shell
groupadd devops creates a group; set the password with passwd deployer
On Debian/Ubuntu, adduser is the friendlier interactive wrapper

subtopics.name: Modifying
points: usermod -aG devops deployer appends a secondary group — the -a is critical
Without -a, usermod -G REPLACES all secondary groups (classic data-loss footgun)
Lock with passwd -l, unlock with passwd -u; expire with chage -E

subtopics.name: Deleting
points: userdel deployer removes the account; -r also removes the home directory
Before deleting: check for running processes and files owned elsewhere (find / -uid N)
Orphaned files keep the numeric UID — reassign or clean them up

subtopics.name: Who is here
points: id shows your UID, primary GID, and all secondary groups
who and w show currently logged-in users and what they are doing
last reads the login history — spot logins at odd hours as a basic intrusion check

subtopics.name: last and login auditing
points: last reads /var/log/wtmp — full login and logout history with timestamps
lastb shows FAILED login attempts — the first check on a suspected box
lastlog shows each user's most recent login — spot dormant accounts waking up

subtopics.name: The distinction
points: su switches to another user and needs THAT user's password
sudo runs a single command as another user with YOUR password plus sudoers permission
sudo logs every invocation — su sessions are far less auditable

subtopics.name: Why sudo wins in production
points: Every sudo invocation is logged with the user, command, and timestamp
sudoers grants per-command privileges — su is all-or-nothing root
No shared root password needed — deprovisioning one user affects nobody else

modules.lab: Create a group devops and a user deployer with a home directory and bash shell; add deployer to devops as a secondary group; lock and unlock the account (passwd -l/-u); verify with id deployer and by reading /etc/passwd and /etc/group. Then delete both.
modules.lab_expected: You can provision and deprovision a user completely from the CLI and know exactly which files change.
modules.interview_q: How do you add an existing user to a group without removing their other groups? Where is password info stored?
modules.interview_a: usermod -aG group user — the -a (append) is essential, otherwise existing secondary groups are wiped. Account data lives in /etc/passwd, password hashes in /etc/shadow, and group memberships in /etc/group.

modules.name: Processes & Job Control
modules.summary: Viewing and controlling processes: states, signals, jobs, priorities.

subtopics.name: Program vs process
points: A program is code on disk; a process is a running instance loaded into memory
Each process gets its own virtual address space and resource handles
One program can spawn many processes — ten nginx workers are ten processes

subtopics.name: PID and PPID
points: PID uniquely identifies a process; PPID is its parent's PID
PID 1 (systemd on modern distros) is the ancestor of all user-space processes
PID 1 has PPID 0 — it is started directly by the kernel, no parent exists

subtopics.name: State codes
points: R: running or runnable — on CPU or waiting for a timeslice
S: interruptible sleep — waiting for an event; the normal idle state
D: uninterruptible sleep — usually stuck in disk I/O, cannot be killed
T: stopped — suspended by Ctrl+Z or a debugger; Z: zombie — dead, awaiting reaping

subtopics.name: Reading states
points: ps aux shows states in the STAT column; top shows them in the S column
A process stuck in D often means wedged storage, not a CPU problem
Lots of Z states means a buggy parent that never calls wait()

subtopics.name: ps snapshots
points: ps aux and ps -ef give full one-shot process listings
ps aux --sort=-%cpu (or -%mem) surfaces resource hogs instantly
pgrep -f pattern finds PIDs by name — no grep -v grep gymnastics needed

subtopics.name: top and htop
points: Live, sortable view of CPU, memory, runtime, and command; q quits
htop adds mouse support, a tree view (F5), and easy signal sending (F9)
Watch the load averages and %wa (I/O wait) in the header, not just the process list

subtopics.name: Job control keys
points: Appending & launches a command in the background, freeing the prompt
Ctrl+Z suspends the foreground job; jobs lists the shell's background jobs
bg resumes a job in the background; fg brings one to the foreground
Ctrl+C sends SIGINT to the foreground process — the polite interrupt

subtopics.name: Scope limits
points: jobs only sees the current shell's jobs — use ps for every process on the system
Background jobs die with the shell unless protected (nohup, disown, or tmux)
For persistent work, tmux/screen beats raw job control

subtopics.name: The essential signals
points: 15 SIGTERM: polite shutdown request — always try this first
9 SIGKILL: unconditional kill, cannot be caught or ignored — last resort, no cleanup runs
1 SIGHUP: historically hangup; daemons conventionally reload config on it
2 SIGINT: what Ctrl+C sends; list every signal with kill -l

subtopics.name: Kill tools and etiquette
points: kill PID targets one process; killall name and pkill -f pattern target by name
Escalation order: SIGTERM, wait a few seconds, then SIGKILL only if needed
Never SIGKILL a database or filesystem-heavy app first — you risk corruption

subtopics.name: nice and renice
points: Niceness ranges from -20 (highest priority) to 19 (lowest); default is 0
nice -n 19 backup.sh launches politely; renice adjusts a running process
Only root can raise priority (negative nice) — anyone can be nice

subtopics.name: Zombie, orphan, daemon
points: Zombie: dead child whose parent never reaped it — kill the parent, not the zombie
Orphan: parent died and init adopted it — usually harmless
Daemon: background service detached from any terminal (sshd, cron)

modules.lab: Start sleep 600 in the background, suspend a foreground sleep 600 with Ctrl+Z and resume it in the background with bg, list jobs, bring one to the foreground and kill it with Ctrl+C. Find a sleep PID with pgrep, terminate it gracefully with kill -15, then launch yes with nice -n 19 and observe its priority in top.
modules.lab_expected: You control foreground/background jobs fluently and always try SIGTERM before SIGKILL.
modules.interview_q: What is a zombie process, how do you find one, and how do you get rid of it?
modules.interview_a: A zombie is a dead child process whose parent never reaped its exit status via wait(). Find them with ps aux filtered for Z in the STAT column or the word defunct. You cannot kill a zombie itself — you must kill or restart its parent process.

modules.name: Text Processing, Pipes & Redirection
modules.summary: Streams, redirection, pipes, and the grep/sed/awk text toolkit.

subtopics.name: The viewers
points: cat dumps whole files — fine for small ones, terrible for huge logs
less pages with scrolling and / search — the safe default viewer
head and tail show the ends; tail -f follows a live-growing log file
nl numbers lines; tac prints a file reversed line order

subtopics.name: Choosing the right viewer
points: cat for small files and concatenation; never cat a 2 GB log
less for anything bigger than a screen — search with /, quit with q
head -n 20 and tail -n 50 preview edges; tail -F survives log rotation

subtopics.name: stdin, stdout, stderr
points: 0 stdin: where a program reads input; 1 stdout: normal output; 2 stderr: error output
Keeping them separate is what makes Unix plumbing composable
A program's exit code ($?) is a fourth channel: success or failure type

subtopics.name: Redirection operators
points: > overwrites a file; >> appends; < feeds a file as stdin
2> captures errors to a file; 2>&1 merges stderr into stdout
&>file captures both streams at once; /dev/null is the bit bucket that discards everything

subtopics.name: The pipe operator
points: cmd1 | cmd2 feeds the stdout of the left command as stdin of the right
Each tool does one thing well; chains compose them into data pipelines
tee splits a stream: cmd | tee out.log | nextcmd saves a copy AND continues the pipe

subtopics.name: Pipeline exit codes
points: A pipeline's exit code is the LAST command's by default — earlier failures hide
set -o pipefail makes the pipeline fail if any stage fails
The PIPESTATUS array holds each stage's code for inspection after the fact

subtopics.name: grep essentials
points: Flags: -i case-insensitive, -v invert match, -r recursive, -n line numbers, -c count, -E extended regex
grep -R 'TODO' --include='*.py' . is a daily codebase search
grep -q runs quietly for use in if conditions — output suppressed, exit code kept

subtopics.name: Regex basics
points: ^ anchors to line start, $ to line end, . matches any single character
* means zero or more of the previous, [] defines a character class, backslash escapes
Always quote your patterns — the shell expands unquoted * before grep ever sees it

subtopics.name: cut, sort, uniq
points: cut -d: -f1 slices delimited fields (like usernames from /etc/passwd)
sort orders lines: -n numeric, -r reverse, -u unique
uniq -c counts adjacent duplicates — input MUST be sorted first
Canonical top-N pattern: cut -d' ' -f1 access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr | head

subtopics.name: tr, wc, diff
points: tr 'a-z' 'A-Z' translates characters — quick case conversion
wc -l counts lines, -w words, -c bytes
diff -u shows unified differences between files — the readable format

subtopics.name: sed the stream editor
points: Substitution: sed 's/old/new/g' file transforms text in a stream
-i edits files in place — always backup first with -i.bak
Use for mechanical transforms: sed -i 's/debug=false/debug=true/' *.conf

subtopics.name: awk the field processor
points: Field-oriented: awk -F: '{print $1}' /etc/passwd prints usernames
Pattern-action pairs: awk '$3 > 1000' filters on conditions
The most programmable of the three — full variables, arithmetic, and formatting

modules.lab: On a 1000+ line fake web-access log: (1) find all 404 lines case-insensitively and count them; (2) extract the IP field, sort, and produce a top-10 offender list with counts (cut | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr | head); (3) redirect errors of a failing find / to /dev/null while saving results to a file with tee.
modules.lab_expected: You build multi-stage pipelines without hesitation and correctly separate stdout from stderr.
modules.interview_q: Explain the difference between grep, sed, and awk — when would you use each?
modules.interview_a: grep filters lines matching a pattern. sed edits streams — substitution, deletion, and transformation across text. awk is field-based processing and reporting, the most programmable of the three. Rule of thumb: find it with grep, change it with sed, report on columns with awk.

modules.name: Vim & Nano
modules.summary: Editing files on headless servers with nano and vim.

subtopics.name: The server reality
points: Production servers have no GUI — config edits happen over SSH in a terminal
vim/vi is guaranteed present on virtually every Unix system ever shipped
nano is friendlier where installed, but you cannot count on it remotely

subtopics.name: vi is the universal fallback
points: POSIX requires vi on every compliant system — it is always there
Minimal containers and rescue shells often ship ONLY vi
If you can drive vi, you can edit configs on any machine on earth

subtopics.name: Basics
points: nano file opens for editing — just type, shortcuts are shown on screen
^O writes out (saves), ^X exits (^ means Ctrl)
Self-teaching interface makes it the safe pick for quick edits

subtopics.name: nano's best shortcuts
points: Ctrl+O writes out, Ctrl+X exits, Ctrl+W searches, Ctrl+K cuts a line
Ctrl+G opens built-in help — nano teaches itself
Alt+U undoes — nano is friendlier than its reputation suggests

subtopics.name: The modal model
points: Normal mode: keys are commands — the default state on open, your safe home base
Insert mode: keys type text — enter with i, a, or o; leave with Esc
Visual mode (v): select text for operations; Command-line mode (:): ex commands at the bottom

subtopics.name: Mode awareness habits
points: Esc returns to Normal mode — tap it twice when lost, it is always safe
The -- INSERT -- indicator at the bottom shows your current mode
Most vim confusion comes from typing commands while stuck in Insert mode

subtopics.name: Movement
points: hjkl move like arrow keys; w/b jump by word; 0/$ jump to line ends
gg goes to file top, G to file bottom; /pattern searches, n jumps to next match
Counts multiply commands: 5dd deletes five lines, 3j moves down three

subtopics.name: Editing primitives
points: i insert before cursor, a append after, o open a new line below
x deletes a character, dd cuts a line, yy yanks (copies), p pastes
u undoes, Ctrl+r redoes — mistakes are cheap

subtopics.name: Exiting correctly
points: :w saves, :q quits, :wq or ZZ saves and quits
:q! abandons all changes — Esc then :q! always escapes when stuck
Getting trapped in vim is a rite of passage; now you know the exit

subtopics.name: Search and replace
points: :%s/old/new/g replaces across the whole file; add c to confirm each one
Always copy real configs before editing: cp nginx.conf nginx.conf.bak
vimtutor (ships with vim) is the canonical 30-minute drill — run it once

modules.lab: Copy /etc/hosts to ~/lab8/hosts (never edit the real one directly). In vim: jump to the last line with G, add an entry below with o, search for localhost with /, replace all occurrences with :%s, undo with u, then save and quit. Repeat the same edit in nano for comparison.
modules.lab_expected: You can open, edit, search, replace, save, and exit in vim without getting stuck — the single most practical server skill.
modules.interview_q: You are SSH'd into a server with only vi available. How do you search, replace all occurrences of a string, and save-and-quit?
modules.interview_a: /pattern searches (n for next match), :%s/old/new/g replaces all occurrences, :wq or ZZ saves and quits, :q! quits discarding changes.

phases.name: System Administration
phases.tagline: Packages, storage, networking, services, scheduling — running real systems

modules.name: Package Management
modules.summary: Installing and managing software with apt/dnf across distro families.

subtopics.name: Core concepts
points: Packages bundle software plus metadata and install scripts into one unit
Repositories are versioned online collections the manager downloads from
Automatic dependency resolution is the killer feature over manual installs

subtopics.name: The two families
points: Debian/Ubuntu: apt is the high-level tool, dpkg the low-level one; .deb files
RHEL/Fedora: dnf (modern yum) is high-level, rpm is low-level; .rpm files
Concepts transfer 1:1 — only the command names change

subtopics.name: The commands
points: apt update refreshes the package index — changes no installed software
apt upgrade installs newer versions of everything installed
apt install/remove/purge manage packages; purge also deletes configuration files
apt search and apt show discover and inspect packages

subtopics.name: dpkg low level
points: dpkg -l lists installed packages; dpkg -L pkg lists the files it installed
dpkg -i file.deb installs a local package without dependency resolution
Classic confusion: update is NOT upgrade — update alone changes nothing

subtopics.name: The commands
points: dnf install/remove/search/info/repolist mirror the apt workflow
rpm -qa lists everything installed; rpm -ql pkg lists its files; rpm -qi shows info
dnf is the modern yum — same concepts, better dependency solver

subtopics.name: dnf extras
points: dnf provides '*/nginx' finds which package owns a file
dnf history reviews and undoes past transactions
dnf check-update lists available updates without installing anything

subtopics.name: Adding sources
points: Ubuntu PPAs (add-apt-repository) and RHEL's EPEL add community packages
Repo files live in /etc/apt/sources.list.d/ and /etc/yum.repos.d/
Third-party repos run install scripts as root — verify trust before adding

subtopics.name: Modern formats
points: snap and flatpak bundle dependencies for desktop apps
Servers rarely need them; know they exist for completeness
Containers (Docker) have largely replaced exotic packaging on servers

modules.lab: On Ubuntu/Debian: apt update, install htop and tree, run apt show htop, list which files the package installed (dpkg -L htop), then remove it with purge. On a RHEL-family VM or container: repeat with dnf install htop, rpm -ql htop, dnf remove htop.
modules.lab_expected: You can install, inspect, and cleanly remove software on both major distro families and explain update vs upgrade.
modules.interview_q: What is the difference between apt update and apt upgrade? Between rpm and dnf/yum?
modules.interview_a: update only refreshes the local package index; upgrade actually installs newer versions. rpm operates on local .rpm files with no dependency resolution; dnf/yum resolve and fetch dependencies from repositories.

modules.name: Archiving & Compression
modules.summary: Bundling and compressing files with tar, gzip, and friends.

subtopics.name: The distinction
points: tar bundles many files into one archive — no compression by itself
gzip/bzip2/xz compress a single stream of bytes
.tar.gz means a tar archive piped through gzip — the classic pairing

subtopics.name: Common extensions decoded
points: .tar.gz / .tgz: tarred then gzipped — the Linux standard
.tar.bz2: bzip2 compression; .tar.xz: xz compression, smallest size
.zip: Windows-compatible; .7z: high ratio via p7zip

subtopics.name: Flag mnemonics
points: c create, x extract, t list contents, f file (always followed by the archive name)
v verbose, z gzip, j bzip2, J xz — compression flags pair with c/x
Create: tar -czf site.tar.gz site/; extract: tar -xzf site.tar.gz; inspect: tar -tzf site.tar.gz

subtopics.name: Extraction safety
points: Always list (-t) before extracting — archives can contain absolute paths or ../ traversals
Extract into an empty directory first when the source is untrusted
--strip-components=1 drops a top-level folder on extract; -C dir chooses the destination

subtopics.name: The trade-off ladder
points: gzip/gunzip: fast with decent ratio — the default choice
bzip2/bunzip2: smaller files, slower — good for archives
xz/unxz: smallest files, slowest — best for distribution
zip/unzip: Windows-compatible format for cross-platform sharing

subtopics.name: Choosing quickly
points: Need speed? gzip. Need size? xz. Need balance? bzip2
Compressing already-compressed media (jpg, mp4) wastes CPU for zero gain
For backups prefer tar plus one compressor over zip — permissions survive

modules.lab: Create ~/lab10/site/{css,js,img} with several files. Create site-backup.tar.gz, list its contents without extracting (tar tzf), extract into ~/lab10/restore/, verify with diff -r. Create a .tar.bz2 of the same tree and compare the two archive sizes.
modules.lab_expected: You never extract an archive blind — you list first — and you know which flag pairs with which compression.
modules.interview_q: How do you create and extract a .tar.gz? How do you list contents without extracting?
modules.interview_a: tar -czf archive.tar.gz dir/ creates; tar -xzf archive.tar.gz extracts; tar -tzf archive.tar.gz lists contents without extracting.

modules.name: Disks, Partitions, Filesystems, Mount & LVM
modules.summary: Partitions, filesystems, mounting, and LVM storage layering.

subtopics.name: Device naming
points: /dev/sda for SATA, /dev/nvme0n1 for NVMe, /dev/vda for virtual disks
Partitions append numbers: sda1, nvme0n1p1 (note the p on NVMe)
lsblk draws the device → partition → mount tree; blkid shows UUIDs and types

subtopics.name: lsblk and blkid in practice
points: lsblk -f adds filesystem types and labels to the tree view
blkid prints UUIDs — copy these into /etc/fstab, never /dev names
lsblk -d shows only disks, hiding partitions for a clean overview

subtopics.name: Tools and schemes
points: fdisk handles MBR; gdisk and parted handle GPT
MBR: 4 primary partitions max, 2 TB limit — legacy only
GPT: 128 partitions, enormous disks — the modern default
Practice ONLY on loop devices or disposable VMs — wrong-disk partitioning destroys data

subtopics.name: MBR vs GPT deep cut
points: MBR: 4 primary partitions max, 2 TB disk limit, bootloader in the first 512 bytes
GPT: 128 partitions by default, 9 ZB max, protective MBR for legacy tools
New systems should always use GPT — MBR is for legacy BIOS edge cases

subtopics.name: Creating and choosing
points: mkfs.ext4 /dev/sda1 writes a filesystem onto a partition
ext4: the general Linux default; xfs: RHEL default, excels at large files and scale
vfat: for USB sticks and EFI partitions where cross-OS compatibility matters
A partition without a filesystem is just raw unusable space

subtopics.name: Tuning and checking
points: tune2fs -l shows ext4 superblock details and mount counts
fsck checks and repairs filesystems — run on UNMOUNTED volumes only
xfs_repair is the xfs equivalent; never fsck a mounted filesystem

subtopics.name: Manual mounts
points: mount /dev/sda1 /mnt/data attaches it to the tree; umount detaches
umount fails if the mount is busy — lsof +D /mnt/data finds the culprit
df -h shows usage per mounted filesystem; findmnt is the readable tree view

subtopics.name: Persistent mounts with fstab
points: /etc/fstab mounts filesystems at boot — the persistence contract
Use UUID= entries (stable) instead of /dev names (can reorder across reboots)
After editing fstab, always run mount -a to verify BEFORE rebooting — a bad fstab can halt boot

topics.name: df vs du and inode exhaustion

subtopics.name: Two different questions
points: df -h: how much free space per filesystem
du -sh dir: how much space a directory tree actually uses
Classic puzzle: df says 100% full but du shows little — deleted files still held open by processes

subtopics.name: Diagnosing the discrepancy
points: lsof | grep deleted reveals open-but-deleted files eating space
Restarting the holding process (or truncating via : > file) frees it
Also check df -i — exhausted inodes block new files despite free gigabytes

subtopics.name: The PV → VG → LV stack
points: PV (physical volume): a raw disk or partition initialized with pvcreate
VG (volume group): pooled storage from one or more PVs
LV (logical volume): a carvable virtual partition from the pool
Decouples filesystems from physical disks — resize without repartitioning

subtopics.name: Extending volumes
points: lvextend -r -L +5G /dev/vgdata/lvdata grows the volume AND filesystem online
The -r flag is the magic — without it you must resize the filesystem separately
Shrinking is riskier and often needs unmounting — plan generously instead

subtopics.name: Purpose
points: Disk-backed overflow for RAM; view with swapon -s or free -h
On RAM-rich modern servers, small swap mainly buys OOM grace and hibernation
Heavy swap use (si/so in vmstat) means the box needs more RAM, not more swap

subtopics.name: Swap in practice
points: swapon -s and free -h show current swap usage
A swap FILE (fallocate + mkswap) works when repartitioning is impossible
vm.swappiness tunes eagerness: 10 for servers, 60 is the desktop default

modules.lab: In a VM (never on a host disk): create a 1 GB file with dd, attach it as a loop device with losetup, partition it with fdisk (GPT, one partition), format as ext4, mount at /mnt/lab11, write a file, add a UUID-based /etc/fstab entry, then run mount -a to verify persistence. Separately, build an LVM stack on a second loop device (PV → VG vgdata → LV lvdata), format, and mount it.
modules.lab_expected: You can take a raw block device from partitioned to formatted to persistently mounted, and you understand the LVM layering.
modules.interview_q: A disk shows 100% full but du shows little usage — what could cause that? How do you extend an LVM logical volume?
modules.interview_a: Deleted-but-still-open files held by processes (check lsof | grep deleted), or inode exhaustion (df -i). Extend with lvextend -r -L +5G /dev/vg/lv — the -r flag resizes the filesystem online.

modules.name: Networking Essentials
modules.summary: IP addressing, DNS, connectivity testing, SSH transfer, and firewalls.

subtopics.name: IPv4 and CIDR
points: 32-bit dotted quads; the netmask/CIDR split defines network vs host portion
192.168.1.0/24 means 254 usable hosts — /24, /16, /8 are the common masks
Gateway is the router to other networks; get IP, mask, and gateway from ip a and ip r

subtopics.name: DNS resolution
points: Names resolve to IPs via resolvers listed in /etc/resolv.conf
/etc/hosts overrides DNS locally — checked before any resolver
getent hosts name tests resolution through the real system stack

subtopics.name: Modern replacement
points: ip a shows addresses, ip r shows the routing table, ip link shows interfaces
Replaces the deprecated ifconfig and route — learn ip, not the old tools
ip -br a gives a terse one-line-per-interface summary

subtopics.name: Everyday ip one-liners
points: ip -br a gives a terse one-line-per-interface summary for scripts
ip r get 8.8.8.8 shows which route and interface a packet would take
ip link set eth0 up/down administratively toggles interfaces

subtopics.name: Layer by layer
points: ping tests L3 reachability — but ICMP is often firewalled, so no reply does not equal down
curl -v https://example.com tests the full HTTP stack and shows status codes and TLS
curl -I fetches headers only — a quick health check
traceroute/mtr shows the path packets take and exactly where they die

subtopics.name: When ping lies
points: Many firewalls drop ICMP — no reply does not prove the host is down
Use TCP probes (nc -zv, curl) when ICMP is filtered
mtr combines ping and traceroute for live path diagnosis

subtopics.name: ss, the socket detective
points: ss -tulnp lists listening TCP/UDP ports with the owning process names
First check for any 'service unreachable' report — is anything even listening?
States to know: LISTEN (waiting), ESTAB (connected), TIME-WAIT (closing)

subtopics.name: Probing ports
points: nc -zv host port is a quick TCP connectivity probe
Distinguishes 'host down' from 'port closed' from 'firewall drop'
Pairs with ss: probe from outside, verify the listener inside

subtopics.name: ssh essentials
points: ssh user@host opens an encrypted remote shell; -p sets the port, -i selects a key file
First connection asks to trust the host key — verify it out-of-band in production
SSH is also the transport for scp, sftp, rsync, and git — learn it once, use it everywhere

subtopics.name: Moving files
points: scp file user@host:/path is simple but restarts from zero on failure
rsync -avz is resumable, transfers only deltas, and preserves permissions — the pro choice
sftp gives an interactive FTP-like session over the SSH channel

subtopics.name: ufw on Debian/Ubuntu
points: Human-friendly frontend: ufw allow 22/tcp, ufw deny 8080
ufw status verbose shows the effective ruleset
Sane baseline: default-deny incoming, allow only needed ports

subtopics.name: firewalld on RHEL
points: firewall-cmd --add-port=8080/tcp --permanent, then --reload to apply
Zones (public, dmz, trusted) separate interfaces by trust level
Classic gotcha: forgetting --permanent means rules vanish on reboot

subtopics.name: The layers that matter
points: L1 physical, L2 link (MAC addresses), L3 network (IP), L4 transport (TCP/UDP ports), L7 application (HTTP, SSH)
Troubleshoot bottom-up: link → IP → route → port → application
Never debug at L7 when L3 is broken — the model saves hours of guessing

subtopics.name: Mapping tools to layers
points: L1: ethtool and dmesg for link state; L2: ip link, arp table
L3: ping and ip r; L4: ss, nc, and TCP probes
L7: curl -v, openssl s_client, and application logs

modules.lab: (1) Use ip a and ip r to document your IP, netmask in CIDR, gateway, and DNS servers. (2) curl -I https://example.com and explain the status line. (3) Run ss -tulnp and identify which process listens on port 22. (4) scp a file to and from a second VM or container over SSH. (5) With ufw: allow port 8080, verify with status verbose, deny it again.
modules.lab_expected: You can describe any machine's network identity, test connectivity at each layer, and move files securely between hosts.
modules.interview_q: A user says 'the website is down.' Walk me through your network troubleshooting steps.
modules.interview_a: Bottom-up: ping the host (L3), verify DNS resolution (getent hosts), curl -v to test the HTTP layer and read the status code, ss -tulnp on the server to confirm the service is listening, then check the firewall. Isolate layer by layer instead of guessing.

modules.name: systemd Services & Logs
modules.summary: Managing services with systemd and reading logs with journalctl.

subtopics.name: Role
points: The first process started by the kernel and the parent of everything in user space
Manages services, mounts, timers, sockets, and boot targets in one framework
Replaced SysV init scripts with declarative unit files

subtopics.name: Why PID 1 is special
points: The kernel panics if PID 1 dies — it must never exit
systemd reaps orphaned processes adopted from dead parents
ps -p 1 confirms the init system; systemd --version shows its release

subtopics.name: Unit types
points: .service runs daemons, .timer schedules, .socket activates on connection, .target groups boot states
Admin unit files live in /etc/systemd/system and override vendor files in /lib/systemd/system
Never edit vendor units directly — use overrides via systemctl edit

subtopics.name: Service lifecycle
points: start/stop/restart/reload/status control the running state right now
enable/disable controls auto-start at boot — independent of current state
mask symlinks a unit to /dev/null, blocking even manual starts — stronger than disable
After editing any unit: systemctl daemon-reload, or systemd ignores your changes

subtopics.name: Targets vs runlevels
points: multi-user.target is the modern runlevel 3 (text multi-user)
graphical.target is the modern runlevel 5 (with display manager)
systemctl get-default and set-default inspect and change the boot target

subtopics.name: Anatomy of a unit
points: [Unit]: Description= and After=network.target declare identity and ordering
[Service]: ExecStart=/full/path (absolute paths only!), Restart=on-failure for resilience
[Install]: WantedBy=multi-user.target hooks it into the boot target
Type=simple is the common default; no shell features in ExecStart unless you wrap with /bin/bash -c

subtopics.name: Common service directives
points: Restart=on-failure with RestartSec=5s makes flaky apps self-heal
User= and Group= drop privileges — never run services as root unnecessarily
EnvironmentFile=/etc/myapp/env keeps secrets out of the unit file

subtopics.name: Querying the journal
points: journalctl -u nginx: logs for one service; -b: this boot only; -f: follow live
--since '1 hour ago' and -p err filter by time and priority
Structured and indexed — far faster than grepping flat files for service history

subtopics.name: Journal power filters
points: journalctl -p err -b shows only errors from the current boot
journalctl --since '09:00' --until '10:00' slices precise time windows
journalctl --disk-usage reports size; --vacuum-size=100M caps growth

subtopics.name: Where things live
points: /var/log/syslog (Debian) or /var/log/messages (RHEL): general system log
auth.log/secure: authentication events — first place for login issues
dmesg: the kernel ring buffer — hardware and driver messages in boot order

subtopics.name: logrotate
points: Rotates, compresses, and prunes logs so they never fill the disk
Configured in /etc/logrotate.conf and /etc/logrotate.d/
A missing logrotate config on a chatty app is a slow-motion disk-full incident

subtopics.name: The drill
points: 1. systemctl status — is it running? enabled? what was the last error?
2. journalctl -u <service> — the service's own story
3. Config syntax check, port conflicts (ss -tulnp), file permissions, missing dependencies
Always in this order — it eliminates whole categories in seconds

subtopics.name: Beyond the basics
points: Check SELinux or AppArmor denials with ausearch or dmesg when permissions look right
Verify the binary actually exists at the ExecStart path — typos are common
Run the command manually as the service's User= account to catch environment issues

modules.lab: Write a systemd unit ~/lab13/hello.service that runs a script logging a timestamp every 10 seconds (install to /etc/systemd/system/, daemon-reload, enable and start it). Then break the script's path on purpose, run systemctl status and journalctl -u hello.service -n 20 to diagnose, fix it, and confirm with journalctl -f.
modules.lab_expected: You can create, enable, debug, and read logs for any service — the core daily sysadmin loop.
modules.interview_q: What is the difference between systemctl disable and systemctl mask? A service will not start — how do you troubleshoot?
modules.interview_a: disable stops auto-start at boot but still allows manual start; mask symlinks the unit to /dev/null, blocking even manual starts. Troubleshoot: systemctl status, then journalctl -u for the service's logs, then check config syntax, port conflicts with ss -tulnp, file permissions, and missing dependencies.

modules.name: Task Scheduling
modules.summary: Scheduling one-off and recurring jobs with at and cron.

subtopics.name: How cron works
points: The crond daemon wakes every minute and runs entries whose time matches
Five fields: minute, hour, day-of-month, month, day-of-week — * means every
The schedule is a contract: if the machine is off at that minute, the run is skipped (see anacron/systemd timers for catch-up)

subtopics.name: Reading expressions
points: */15 * * * * runs every 15 minutes; 30 2 * * 1 runs 2:30 AM on Mondays
0 0 1 * * runs at midnight on the first of each month
Lists (1,15), ranges (9-17), and steps (*/10) compose freely

subtopics.name: User crontabs
points: crontab -e edits your entries; crontab -l lists; crontab -r REMOVES them all with no undo
No username field — entries run as you
Export a backup (crontab -l > backup) before any -r

subtopics.name: System crontabs
points: /etc/crontab and /etc/cron.d/ include a username field for the entry to run as
/etc/cron.hourly, daily, weekly, monthly run any executable script placed inside
Know which file you are editing — wrong file means silent non-execution

subtopics.name: The minimal environment
points: Cron runs with a tiny PATH, no aliases, and no interactive shell initialization
Rule: use absolute paths for everything, or set PATH and needed variables at the crontab top
Scripts that work in your shell fail in cron almost always because of environment
Capture output: * * * * * /opt/job.sh >> /var/log/job.log 2>&1 — silent cron is undebuggable cron

subtopics.name: Debugging silent cron
points: Redirect output to a log: * * * * * /opt/job.sh >> /var/log/job.log 2>&1
Check /var/log/cron or journalctl -u cron for execution evidence
Test the exact command with env -i to simulate cron's bare environment

subtopics.name: Usage
points: echo '/opt/backup.sh' | at 02:00 tomorrow schedules a single future run
atq lists the queue; atrm <n> removes a queued job
Perfect for run-this-once-later without committing a permanent cron entry

subtopics.name: at in practice
points: at now + 1 hour accepts natural-language time specs
at -c <jobid> prints the full script that will execute — verify before it runs
Batch queues (at -q b) defer jobs until load average drops — for heavy work

subtopics.name: The modern alternative
points: A .timer unit paired with a .service: OnCalendar= for wall-clock, OnBootSec=/OnUnitActiveSec= for relative triggers
Advantages: journal-integrated logging, dependency ordering, persistent catch-up runs
Inspect with systemctl list-timers — know they exist even if cron remains your default

subtopics.name: Timer vs cron cheat sheet
points: Use cron for simple recurring shell tasks — it exists everywhere
Use timers when you need logging, dependencies, or catch-up runs
systemctl list-timers --all shows upcoming and recently elapsed runs

modules.lab: Schedule a cron job that appends date to ~/lab14/heartbeat.log every minute (* * * * *), wait 3 minutes, verify 3 lines exist, then remove it. Schedule a one-off at job 2 minutes in the future that creates ~/lab14/at-works.txt, and confirm it with atq.
modules.lab_expected: You can write a correct 5-field cron expression from memory and you know cron jobs run with a minimal environment (use absolute paths).
modules.interview_q: What does */15 * * * * mean, and what is the difference between cron and systemd timers?
modules.interview_a: Every 15 minutes. cron is the simple, ubiquitous time-based scheduler; systemd timers add calendar and monotonic triggers, dependency handling, and journal-integrated logging.

phases.name: Automation
phases.tagline: Environment mastery and Bash scripting — making the machine work for you

modules.name: Environment Variables & Shell Config
modules.summary: Environment variables, PATH, and shell startup files.

subtopics.name: The distinction
points: Shell variables exist only in the current shell instance
Environment variables are exported and inherited by child processes
export VAR=value promotes a shell variable; VAR=value cmd sets it for one command only
env and printenv list the environment; unset removes a variable

subtopics.name: Export in practice
points: export EDITOR=vim makes every child program use vim
Variables set without export stay invisible to scripts you launch
printenv VAR checks one variable; env | grep PATH filters the list

subtopics.name: How commands are found
points: PATH is a colon-separated list of directories searched in order
which python3 shows which directory won the search
Add personal bins with export PATH="$HOME/bin:$PATH" — prepend, do not append blindly
Never put . (current directory) first in PATH — a classic privilege-escalation trap

subtopics.name: PATH debugging
points: type -a python3 shows EVERY match in PATH search order
hash -r clears bash's cached command locations after new installs
Command not found despite being installed usually means a PATH or re-login issue

subtopics.name: Login vs interactive shells
points: ~/.bash_profile (or ~/.profile) runs for login shells — SSH sessions, console logins
~/.bashrc runs for interactive non-login shells — new terminal tabs
/etc/profile and /etc/bash.bashrc are the system-wide counterparts
Rule of thumb: environment and login-time setup in profile; aliases, functions, and prompt in bashrc

subtopics.name: Applying changes with source
points: Editing a startup file changes nothing until it is loaded
source ~/.bashrc (or . ~/.bashrc) applies it to the current shell
Scripts run in subshells — their variables die with them unless the script is sourced

subtopics.name: Aliases
points: alias ll='ls -lh' creates shortcuts; unalias removes them
Make permanent by defining in ~/.bashrc
Functions beat aliases for anything taking arguments or containing logic

subtopics.name: Customizing PS1
points: The prompt string supports escapes: \u user, \h host, \w working dir, \$ prompt char
Colorize carefully — unescaped sequences break line wrapping; wrap in \[ \]
A informative prompt (user@host:path + git branch) prevents wrong-machine mistakes

modules.lab: Add ~/lab15/bin to your PATH persistently via ~/.bashrc, create an executable hello script there, source ~/.bashrc, and run hello from any directory. Create an alias ll='ls -lh' and make it permanent. Then demonstrate the difference between VAR=x ./script.sh and export VAR=x for child-process visibility.
modules.lab_expected: You understand exactly where to put persistent config and why source is needed after editing.
modules.interview_q: What is the difference between ~/.bashrc and ~/.bash_profile? Why does a cron job not see your aliases?
modules.interview_a: .bash_profile runs for login shells; .bashrc for interactive non-login shells. cron runs non-interactive with a minimal environment — no aliases, tiny PATH — so scripts must use absolute paths and explicit environment variables.

modules.name: Bash Scripting
modules.summary: Writing robust Bash scripts: variables, tests, loops, functions.

subtopics.name: Shebang and execution
points: #!/bin/bash on line one tells the kernel which interpreter to use
chmod +x makes the script executable; ./script.sh runs it
Scripts can also run via bash script.sh — useful when the execute bit is missing

subtopics.name: The robust header
points: set -euo pipefail: -e exits on first error, -u fails on unset variables
-o pipefail makes a pipeline fail if ANY stage fails, not just the last
This trio converts silent breakage into loud, debuggable failure

subtopics.name: Assignment and reference
points: name=value with NO spaces around =; reference with $name or ${name}
today=$(date +%F) captures command output; $((2 + 2)) does arithmetic
'single quotes' are literal; "double quotes" expand variables; prefer $(...) over backticks

subtopics.name: The quoting rule
points: ALWAYS quote variables: "$var" — unquoted values undergo word-splitting and globbing
Filenames with spaces are the classic victim of unquoted variables
This single habit eliminates the most common class of shell bugs

subtopics.name: Arguments
points: $1 is the first argument, $@ is all arguments (quote it!), $# is the count
shift drops $1, moving $2 into its place — handy for option parsing loops
read -p 'Name: ' name takes interactive input from the user

subtopics.name: Exit codes
points: exit 0 means success; any non-zero value signals a failure type
$? holds the previous command's exit code — check it immediately
Scripts should exit non-zero with a usage message on invalid input

subtopics.name: Test constructs
points: [ ] is the POSIX test; [[ ]] is Bash's safer version (no word-splitting, supports =~ regex)
Strings: -z empty, -n non-empty, = and != compare; numbers: -eq -ne -lt -le -gt -ge
Files: -f regular file, -d directory, -e exists, -r/-w/-x permission checks
if grep -q pattern file; then — test a command's exit code directly, no brackets needed

subtopics.name: case statements
points: case $1 in start) ...;; stop) ...;; *) usage;; esac dispatches cleanly on patterns
Each branch ends with ;; — forgetting it is the classic syntax error
Ideal for subcommand-style scripts (service scripts, CLIs)

subtopics.name: Loops
points: for f in *.log; do ...; done iterates globs or lists
while read -r line; do ...; done < file is the safe file-reading idiom (-r keeps backslashes)
break exits the loop, continue skips to the next iteration; seq or {1..10} generate ranges

subtopics.name: Functions
points: backup() { local src=$1; ...; } — local keeps variables from leaking globally
return sets $? (0–255 only); use echo to return actual data
Functions turn repeated blocks into named, testable units

subtopics.name: Tools
points: bash -x script.sh traces every executed line with a + prefix — the fastest debugger
bash -n checks syntax without executing anything
shellcheck (install it) lints scripts like a senior reviewer — run it on every script

subtopics.name: Defensive scripting habits
points: Quote every variable, validate every argument, exit non-zero on misuse
Use mktemp for temporary files — predictable names invite symlink attacks
Timestamp your logs: echo "$(date -Is) starting" >> run.log

modules.lab: Write ~/lab16/backup.sh that takes a directory as $1, validates it exists (exit 1 with a usage message otherwise), creates a timestamped tar.gz in ~/backups/, keeps only the 5 newest backups (loop + ls -t), and logs each run to a log file. Run it with bash -x to watch execution.
modules.lab_expected: You write defensive scripts: quoted variables, validated arguments, meaningful exit codes — the RHCSA scripting bar (conditionals, loops, $1/$2, processing command output).
modules.interview_q: What does set -euo pipefail do, and why should scripts use "$var" with quotes?
modules.interview_a: -e exits on the first error, -u errors on unset variables, -o pipefail makes pipelines fail if any stage fails. Unquoted variables undergo word-splitting and glob expansion — the classic source of bugs with filenames containing spaces.

phases.name: Security & Mastery
phases.tagline: SSH hardening, boot literacy, and the troubleshooting mindset

modules.name: SSH Keys, sudo & Hardening
modules.summary: SSH key auth, least-privilege sudo, and server hardening basics.

subtopics.name: How it works
points: ssh-keygen -t ed25519 creates a keypair: private key stays on your machine (chmod 600)
The public key goes into ~/.ssh/authorized_keys on each server
At login the server sends a challenge; your client signs it with the private key — the key itself never travels the network
ssh-copy-id user@host installs your public key in one step

subtopics.name: ssh-agent
points: Caches decrypted keys in memory so you type the passphrase once per session
ssh-add loads a key; agent forwarding (-A) is convenient but risky on untrusted hosts
Prefer ProxyJump over agent forwarding for multi-hop access

subtopics.name: sshd_config essentials
points: PermitRootLogin no — attackers cannot even attempt the most-targeted account
PasswordAuthentication no — keys only, immune to password brute-forcing
Consider a non-standard Port to dodge automated scanners (obscurity, not security — layer it)
After changes: restart sshd AND keep a second session open while testing — locking yourself out is the classic mistake

subtopics.name: Brute-force defense
points: fail2ban auto-bans IPs after N failed attempts — cheap, effective
Rate-limiting at the firewall is a complementary layer
Monitor auth.log/secure for probing patterns

subtopics.name: The model
points: su switches to another user and needs THAT user's password
sudo runs one command as another user with YOUR password plus sudoers permission
sudo -i opens a root shell; sudo -l lists exactly what you may run
sudo logs every invocation — su sessions are far less auditable

subtopics.name: Editing sudoers safely
points: ALWAYS edit with visudo — it syntax-checks before saving
A broken sudoers file can lock out all administrative access
Grant narrowly: deployer ALL=(ALL) /usr/bin/systemctl restart nginx beats ALL=(ALL) ALL
Least privilege is the governing principle, not convenience

subtopics.name: The baseline
points: Key-only SSH with root login disabled
Firewall default-deny with only required ports open
Prompt security updates (unattended-upgrades or a patch routine)
Remove or disable every unneeded service — check with ss -tulnp
Least privilege everywhere: users, sudo entries, and file permissions

subtopics.name: Ongoing hygiene
points: Review sudoers and user accounts quarterly — remove the departed promptly
Subscribe to distro security notices; patch on a schedule, not in a panic
Keep off-machine backups and TEST restores — untested backups are wishes

modules.lab: Generate an ed25519 key pair (ssh-keygen -t ed25519), copy the public key to a second VM or container with ssh-copy-id, and log in without a password. Harden the lab server: set PermitRootLogin no and PasswordAuthentication no in sshd_config, restart sshd, and confirm password login is rejected. Create a user with a limited sudoers entry via visudo (allow only systemctl restart nginx) and verify sudo -l shows just that.
modules.lab_expected: You treat password SSH as legacy and can grant least-privilege sudo access safely.
modules.interview_q: How does SSH key authentication work, and what are the first three hardening steps for a new server?
modules.interview_a: The client proves possession of the private key by signing a server challenge; the server verifies the signature against authorized_keys — the private key never crosses the network. First three hardening steps: key-only SSH with root login disabled, firewall default-deny with minimal open ports, and prompt patching with unneeded services removed.

modules.name: Kernel Modules & Boot
modules.summary: Kernel modules, /proc and /sys, and the boot sequence.

subtopics.name: Loadable drivers
points: Drivers compiled as modules keep the core kernel lean; hardware support plugs in at runtime
lsmod lists loaded modules; modinfo shows a module's details and parameters
modprobe loads a module (resolving dependencies); modprobe -r unloads it
Modules live under /lib/modules/$(uname -r)/; depmod rebuilds dependency maps

subtopics.name: Module autoloading
points: Files in /etc/modules-load.d/ list modules to load at boot
Blacklists in /etc/modprobe.d/ prevent unwanted drivers from loading
Rebuild the initramfs after touching early-boot modules or the change may not apply

subtopics.name: Kernel interfaces as files
points: /proc: process info plus kernel stats — cpuinfo, meminfo, per-PID directories
/sys: the kernel object model — devices, drivers, and subsystems as a tree
Both are RAM-backed virtual filesystems: zero disk usage, instant kernel truth
Some /sys files are writable tunables — echoing values changes live kernel behavior

subtopics.name: Handy one-liners
points: grep 'model name' /proc/cpuinfo | head -1 identifies the CPU
head -3 /proc/meminfo gives a quick memory overview
ls /sys/class/net/ lists network interfaces as kernel objects

subtopics.name: Power button to PID 1
points: Firmware (BIOS/UEFI) runs POST, then hands off to the bootloader
GRUB shows the menu and loads the kernel plus initramfs into memory
initramfs: a tiny early filesystem carrying the drivers needed to find the real root
The kernel initializes hardware, mounts the real root filesystem, and starts PID 1 (systemd)

subtopics.name: systemd takes over
points: systemd reaches the default target (multi-user or graphical) and starts all enabled units
The login prompt appears once the target's dependencies are satisfied
Check or change the default with systemctl get-default / set-default

subtopics.name: Reading the boot story
points: dmesg shows the kernel ring buffer — hardware detection in chronological boot order
journalctl -b shows this boot's complete systemd story
Boot trouble? Edit the GRUB entry at boot (press e) or pick an older kernel from the menu

modules.lab: Run lsmod | head, pick a non-critical module, inspect it with modinfo, then unload and reload it (modprobe -r / modprobe) inside a VM. Check your default systemd target, list available targets, and read the first 30 lines of dmesg to identify kernel hardware-detection messages.
modules.lab_expected: You understand that drivers are loadable modules and you can read the boot story from firmware to login prompt.
modules.interview_q: Describe what happens between pressing the power button and the login prompt.
modules.interview_a: Firmware POST, then GRUB loads the kernel and initramfs. The kernel initializes hardware and mounts the real root filesystem, then hands control to systemd (PID 1). systemd reaches the default target (e.g. multi-user.target) and presents the login prompt.

modules.name: Performance & Troubleshooting
modules.summary: Reading system metrics and troubleshooting like a professional.

subtopics.name: What it means
points: The 1, 5, and 15-minute averages of runnable plus uninterruptible processes — system demand
Rule of thumb: sustained load above the CPU core count means queuing
Load 8 on 4 cores is overloaded; load 8 on 16 cores is comfortable
uptime displays it instantly — the first command on any slow box

subtopics.name: Reading the three numbers
points: The 1, 5, and 15-minute trio shows trend — rising means load is growing
Compare against nproc output — the core count is your yardstick
High load with low CPU percent usually means D-state processes stuck on I/O

subtopics.name: The sequence
points: uptime first — load averages versus core count tells if the box is actually busy
top/htop — who eats CPU and RAM; watch %wa for I/O wait
free -h — memory and swap pressure; active swapping means pain
df -h plus iostat for disk full or saturation; ss -tulnp and systemctl confirm services listen and run
journalctl and dmesg last — the logs get the final word; metrics first, hypotheses second

subtopics.name: Document as you go
points: Keep a timestamped timeline of symptoms observed and commands run
Write the incident note BEFORE you forget: symptom, cause, fix
Patterns across incidents reveal systemic fixes — the senior-engineer habit

subtopics.name: Reading top
points: us = user CPU, sy = system CPU, wa = I/O wait — high wa means a storage bottleneck
Sort by %MEM to catch memory leaks; TIME+ reveals cumulative CPU hogs
Load averages sit top-right — correlate them with what the process list shows

subtopics.name: vmstat and iostat
points: vmstat 1: one line per second covering procs, memory, swap (si/so), I/O (bi/bo), CPU
iostat -x: per-device stats — %util near 100% means the disk is saturated
Needs the sysstat package on some distros

subtopics.name: Deeper inspection
points: lsof -i :8080 reveals exactly which process holds a port
ps aux --sort=-%cpu gives a static ranked snapshot for reports
strace -p PID shows live system calls — powerful, use carefully in production

subtopics.name: The method
points: Define the symptom precisely — 'slow' is not a definition
Reproduce it reliably before changing anything
Isolate layer by layer: network, disk, memory, application
Form ONE hypothesis, test it, verify the fix, then document symptom, cause, and fix
Change one thing at a time and keep a timeline — guessing in circles is the expensive failure mode

subtopics.name: Classic scenarios
points: Disk full: df -h, then du -sx /* to find the hog, lsof for deleted-but-open files
Out of memory: dmesg for OOM-killer lines, free -h for pressure evidence
Runaway CPU: top to identify, kill -15 first, escalate to -9 only if needed
Service down: systemctl status, then journalctl -u, then config, ports, permissions

modules.lab: Capstone break/fix on a lab VM: a partner (or a setup script) introduces 3 faults — (1) a runaway yes > /dev/null process, (2) a disk filled with a junk file, (3) a stopped web service. Diagnose each using only uptime, top, df -h/du, systemctl status, and journalctl; fix all three; write a 5-line incident note per fault (symptom, cause, fix).
modules.lab_expected: You follow a repeatable method instead of guessing, and you reach for metrics and logs before Stack Overflow — the DevOps-ready mindset.
modules.interview_q: A production server is slow. Walk me through exactly what you check, in order.
modules.interview_a: uptime (load averages vs CPU count), then top/htop (who is eating CPU/RAM, check I/O wait), free -h (memory and swap pressure), df -h plus iostat (disk full or I/O-bound), ss and service checks if app-specific, and journalctl/dmesg for errors. Metrics first, hypotheses second.
